### Problem: Sorting the Sentence {#sec-lts-p4-a}

::: {.p-statement}

A sentence is words separated by single spaces, no leading/trailing spaces. It is *shuffled* by appending each word's 1-indexed position to its end and rearranging. Given `s` ($2 \le |s| \le 200$; between 1 and 9 words; letters, spaces, and digits `1`–`9`), reconstruct the original sentence.

Source: [LC 1859 · Sorting the Sentence](https://leetcode.com/problems/sorting-the-sentence/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}

Example — `s = "is2 sentence4 This1 a3"`. Output `"This is a sentence"` (each word carries its slot; strip the digits).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Every word already names its own destination: the trailing digit *is* the index. That is the counting-sort situation in its purest form — the key is a small integer in a known range $[1, w]$, so instead of comparing words, write each straight into slot `d-1`. This is @sec-lts-a1's "value as address" with the address handed to us for free.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Sort by the trailing character.** Split on spaces, `sorted(ws, key=lambda w: w[-1])`, then strip the last character of each and join. $O(w \log w)$ comparisons on single characters — the oracle.
2. **Direct placement.** Allocate `out = [None] * w`; for each word write `out[int(w[-1]) - 1] = w[:-1]`; join. $O(n)$, no comparisons at all.

**Invariant.** Because the digits are exactly the permutation $1..w$, after placement every slot holds precisely the word that belonged there, so reading slots left-to-right is the original sentence.
:::

The buttons are in order: lean on a comparison sort of the digits, then drop the comparisons and index directly.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Sort by embedded index

::: {.form-next}
Split into words, order them by their final character (the position digit), strip the digits, join. $O(w \log w)$ time, $O(n)$ space — correct and the baseline.

**Worked example.** `["is2","sentence4","This1","a3"]` sorted by last char → `This1, is2, a3, sentence4` → `"This is a sentence"`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("sent", "sort")
    assert str(final) == "This is a sentence"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def sst1859_sort(s):
    ws = sorted(s.split(), key=lambda w: w[-1])
    return " ".join(w[:-1] for w in ws)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// order words by their trailing position digit, then strip it
string sst1859Sort(string s) {
    vector<string> ws;
    string cur;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (c == ' ') { ws.push_back(cur); cur.clear(); }
        else cur.push_back(c);
    }
    ws.push_back(cur);
    sort(ws.begin(), ws.end(), [](const string& a, const string& b) {
        return a.back() < b.back();
    });
    string res;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < ws.size(); ++i) {
        if (i) res.push_back(' ');
        res += ws[i].substr(0, ws[i].size() - 1);
    }
    return res;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `key=lambda w: w[-1]` compares only the last character, and since every digit is distinct the sort is a total order with no ties. It is $O(w \log w)$ on at most 9 words — trivial — but it is still comparisons, and the digit already tells us the answer outright, which the placement form exploits.

#### Direct placement (counting sort)

::: {.form-next}
Split, then write each word into `out[digit-1]` with its digit removed; join the array. $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space, zero comparisons — the digit is a ready-made array index.

**Worked example.** `out[1]="is"`, `out[4]="sentence"`, `out[0]="This"`, `out[2]="a"` → read slots `This is a sentence`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("sent", "place")
    assert str(final) == "This is a sentence"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-1859-place
def sst1859_place(s):
    ws = s.split()
    out = [None] * len(ws)
    for w in ws:
        out[int(w[-1]) - 1] = w[:-1]
    return " ".join(out)

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 9)
    words = ["".join(random.choice("abcXY") for _ in range(random.randint(1, 5))) for _ in range(n)]
    shuffled = " ".join(words[d - 1] + str(d) for d in random.sample(range(1, n + 1), n))
    assert sst1859_place(shuffled) == " ".join(words)
    assert sst1859_sort(shuffled) == " ".join(words)
assert sst1859_place("is2 sentence4 This1 a3") == "This is a sentence"
assert sst1859_place("Myself2 Me1 I4 and3") == "Me Myself and I"
print("sst1859_place OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// the position digit is the address; write each word into its slot
string sst1859Place(string s) {
    vector<string> ws;
    string cur;
    for (char c : s) {
        if (c == ' ') { ws.push_back(cur); cur.clear(); }
        else cur.push_back(c);
    }
    ws.push_back(cur);
    vector<string> out(ws.size());
    for (string& w : ws) {
        int pos = w.back() - '1';
        out[pos] = w.substr(0, w.size() - 1);
    }
    string res;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < out.size(); ++i) { if (i) res.push_back(' '); res += out[i]; }
    return res;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `out[int(w[-1]) - 1] = w[:-1]` is the whole algorithm: the digit picks the slot, the slice drops it. Because the digits are a permutation of $1..w$, no slot is written twice and none is left `None`, so `" ".join(out)` never sees a gap. The stress test builds a known word list, scrambles it with correct digits, and checks both forms reproduce the original.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Sort by digit** is $O(w \log w)$ time, $O(n)$ space. **Direct placement** is $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. With $w \le 9$ both are effectively linear; placement is the honest counting sort because it compares nothing.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- A single word `Hi1` → `Hi` (one slot, still a valid permutation).
- Words differ in length, so the digit is always the *last* character — never confused with a letter.
- Digits are only `1`–`9`, guaranteeing at most 9 words and a bounded key range.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1528 · Shuffle String](https://leetcode.com/problems/shuffle-string/){difficulty="Easy"} — every character carries its destination index: `out[indices[i]] = s[i]`.
- [LC 1640 · Check Array Formation Through Concatenation](https://leetcode.com/problems/check-array-formation-through-concatenation/){difficulty="Easy"} — values are distinct and small, so index each piece by its first value.
:::
